claims.text: Spin-polarized density functional theory can be used to establish the existence of ferromagnetic ground states.
A ferromagnetic ground state can be identified by showing that a spin-polarized ferromagnetic configuration has lower total energy than a non-magnetic configuration.
The modeled material is a crystalline system initially placed in a high-symmetry, non-magnetic configuration.
The proposed calculation explicitly compares ferromagnetic and non-magnetic electronic configurations.
The simulations are to be performed at zero temperature with periodic boundary conditions.
An exchange-correlation functional capable of treating spin polarization correctly is required.
Electronic exchange and correlation interactions permit spin splitting of the electronic states.
Spin polarization introduces exchange splitting.
Exchange splitting can lower the total energy of a ferromagnetic configuration relative to a non-magnetic state.
Lowering the ferromagnetic configuration's energy relative to the non-magnetic state stabilizes a ferromagnetic ground state.
The spin-polarized ferromagnetic calculation will have significantly lower total energy than the non-spin-polarized calculation.
The spin-polarized calculation will predict a measurable net magnetic moment.
Non-spin-polarized DFT assumes equal populations of spin-up and spin-down electrons.
The non-spin-polarized baseline has no net magnetic moment.
The non-spin-polarized baseline has higher total energy than the ferromagnetic configuration.
The method is most reliable when magnetism arises from itinerant electrons.
Standard spin-polarized DFT may have limited applicability in strongly correlated systems.
Some standard exchange-correlation functionals may fail to capture the physics required to describe magnetism.
The magnitude of energy lowering and the stability of the ferromagnetic state depend on the exchange-correlation functional and material parameters.
Failure to obtain both a lower spin-polarized energy and a significant net magnetic moment would falsify the proposed prediction for the tested material.
